items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “whether a research project can be completed with the time, sources, skills and word count available”?
items.answer: Feasibility
items.markingKey: Feasibility: whether a research project can be completed with the time, sources, skills and word count available. [1]

items.stem: Explain why personal interest matters when choosing a topic such as migration caused by climate change for the research report, and identify one risk.
items.answer: It sustains motivation over many months of independent work, and prior knowledge helps the student ask better questions. Risk: it may lead to bias if the student already holds strong views.
items.markingKey: 1 mark why it matters; 1 mark developed; 1 mark risk [3]

items.stem: Explain why feasibility matters when choosing a topic such as reform of the UN Security Council for the research report, and identify one risk.
items.answer: The student can actually obtain enough credible evidence within the time and word limit. Risk: focusing only on feasibility may produce a safe but unoriginal question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark why it matters; 1 mark developed; 1 mark risk [3]

items.stem: Grace lives in Dubai and has followed debates about corruption in public procurement for two years. A first search finds a report by an independent election-monitoring mission and several news reports, but little local data. Grace wants to research “corruption in public procurement” for the research report. Explain one advantage of choosing a topic of personal interest.
items.answer: Motivation is sustained over a long project and existing knowledge helps frame good questions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Priya scores three possible research topics from 1 to 5 against weighted criteria. Topic | personal interest (weight 2) | academic debate (weight 2) | feasibility (weight 3). lowering the voting age to 16 | 4 | 4 | 5. low voter turnout among young people | 2 | 5 | 4. the under-representation of women in parliaments | 5 | 5 | 5. Calculate the weighted score for each topic and identify the topic Priya should choose.
items.answer: lowering the voting age to 16: 4×2 + 4×2 + 5×3 = 31; low voter turnout among young people: 2×2 + 5×2 + 4×3 = 26; the under-representation of women in parliaments: 5×2 + 5×2 + 5×3 = 35. Choose: the under-representation of women in parliaments.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark all totals; 1 mark choice [3]

items.stem: Assess the claim that feasibility should be the most important factor when choosing a research report topic.
items.answer: For: A topic without accessible evidence cannot be researched properly. Time and word limits are fixed. Against: Without interest, motivation fades over a long project. A topic needs a genuine academic debate and alternative perspectives. Judgement: Feasibility is a necessary condition, but the best topics, e.g. on the spread of online disinformation during elections, combine interest, debate and access to evidence.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Explain why academic context matters when choosing a topic such as disputes over shared rivers for the research report, and identify one risk.
items.answer: An existing debate provides theories, studies and contrasting perspectives to analyse. Risk: a crowded field may make it hard to find an original angle.
items.markingKey: 1 mark why it matters; 1 mark developed; 1 mark risk [3]

items.stem: Freya scores three possible research topics from 1 to 5 against weighted criteria. Topic | personal interest (weight 2) | academic debate (weight 1) | feasibility (weight 3). lowering the voting age to 16 | 5 | 3 | 4. low voter turnout among young people | 4 | 4 | 5. reform of the UN Security Council | 4 | 4 | 3. Calculate the weighted score for each topic and identify the topic Freya should choose.
items.answer: lowering the voting age to 16: 5×2 + 3×1 + 4×3 = 25; low voter turnout among young people: 4×2 + 4×1 + 5×3 = 27; reform of the UN Security Council: 4×2 + 4×1 + 3×3 = 21. Choose: low voter turnout among young people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark all totals; 1 mark choice [3]

items.stem: A proposed research question is: “Is lowering the voting age to 16 good or bad?” What is its main weakness?
options: It has a single factual answer, so no alternative perspectives are possible
It is far too broad to answer in depth in 5,000 words
It leaves its key terms undefined, so it cannot be answered with evidence
It is worded to assume the answer
items.answer: It leaves its key terms undefined, so it cannot be answered with evidence
items.markingKey: It leaves its key terms undefined, so it cannot be answered with evidence. [1]

options: It leaves its key terms undefined, so it cannot be answered with evidence
It invites description rather than evaluation of a debate
It is worded to assume the answer
It has a single factual answer, so no alternative perspectives are possible
items.answer: It invites description rather than evaluation of a debate

items.stem: Rewrite this research question so that it is focused and permits alternative perspectives: “In which year was the first international agreement on migration caused by climate change signed?” Explain how your version improves on it.
items.answer: e.g. “To what extent is it the responsibility of the United Nations member states to address migration caused by climate change?” — the original has a single factual answer, so no alternative perspectives are possible; the new question is contestable, focused and can be answered using evidence from different perspectives (e.g. the government of a low-lying Pacific island state and a populist party in a high-income country).
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused question; 1 mark contestable; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: Rewrite this research question so that it is focused and permits alternative perspectives: “What are the main features of state use of facial recognition surveillance?” Explain how your version improves on it.
items.answer: e.g. “To what extent is state use of facial recognition surveillance best addressed through national rather than international action?” — the original invites description rather than evaluation of a debate; the new question is contestable, focused and can be answered using evidence from different perspectives (e.g. a police chief and a civil liberties group).
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused question; 1 mark contestable; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: Rewrite this research question so that it is focused and permits alternative perspectives: “In which year was the first international agreement on the export of plastic waste to poorer countries signed?” Explain how your version improves on it.
items.answer: e.g. “To what extent is it the responsibility of the national government to address the export of plastic waste to poorer countries?” — the original has a single factual answer, so no alternative perspectives are possible; the new question is contestable, focused and can be answered using evidence from different perspectives (e.g. an environmental NGO in Malaysia and a waste trading company).
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused question; 1 mark contestable; 1 mark explains improvement; 1 mark names perspectives that could be compared [4]

items.stem: Kwame argues that “to what extent” questions are always the best form of research question for the research report. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: They invite judgement and the weighing of perspectives. They allow a qualified conclusion. Against: Other forms (“Should…?”, “How far…?”) can be equally contestable. A “to what extent” question can still be vague or too broad. Judgement: The form matters less than focus, contestability and defined terms; e.g. “Should countries upstream on a shared river need the agreement of downstream countries before building dams?” works without that wording.

items.stem: A student’s research question is “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the parliament should lower the voting age to 16 for all elections?” Explain why the term “benefits” must be defined in the report, and suggest how.

items.stem: Aisha’s proposed research question is: “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the riverside governments should ask a neutral mediator such as the African Union or the World Bank to help?” Explain one type of primary research that could help answer the question.

items.stem: The research report on lowering the voting age to 16 is due at the end of week 26. Tasks, done one after another: literature review 5 weeks, primary research 2 weeks, analysis 3 weeks, drafting 4 weeks, editing and referencing 1 week. What is the latest week by the end of which the student must start?
items.answer: Week 11
items.markingKey: Total 15 weeks; 26 − 15 = 11. [1]

items.stem: A student’s report on state use of facial recognition surveillance must be submitted at the end of week 20. Tasks, done in sequence: literature review 5 weeks, primary research 2 weeks, analysis 3 weeks, drafting 3 weeks, editing and referencing 2 weeks. The supervisor advises leaving 2 weeks’ contingency. Calculate the total time needed and the latest week by the end of which the student must start, including the contingency.
items.answer: Total = 15 weeks; with contingency 17 weeks; latest start = end of week 20 − 17 = week 3.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark contingency added; 1 mark latest start [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that a detailed research proposal is the key to a successful research report on migration caused by climate change.
items.answer: For: It clarifies the question, methods and sources before work begins. A timeline and milestones prevent last-minute work. Against: Research often changes direction as evidence is found, so plans must be flexible. Success depends on the quality of analysis and evaluation, which a plan cannot guarantee. Judgement: A proposal is necessary but not sufficient; it should be revised as the research log records changes.

items.stem: A student’s report on lowering the voting age to 16 must be submitted at the end of week 26. Tasks, done in sequence: literature review 5 weeks, primary research 4 weeks, analysis 3 weeks, drafting 3 weeks, editing and referencing 1 week. The supervisor advises leaving 2 weeks’ contingency. Calculate the total time needed and the latest week by the end of which the student must start, including the contingency. Explain why the contingency is important for primary research.
items.answer: Total = 16 weeks; with contingency 18 weeks; latest start = end of week 26 − 18 = week 8. Primary research is often delayed (low response rates, ethical approval, cancelled interviews), so slack protects the deadline.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark contingency added; 1 mark latest start; 1 mark reason delays are likely; 1 mark effect on deadline [5]

items.stem: A student plans interviews with people affected by state use of facial recognition surveillance. Explain why protection from harm is important and how the student could ensure it.
items.answer: Protection from harm means that participants should not suffer physical or psychological harm, such as distress or embarrassment; this protects participants and the credibility of the research. The student could explain it at the start, record it on a consent form and follow it when storing and reporting data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark why important; 1 mark practical step [3]

items.stem: Kenji plans to research the export of plastic waste to poorer countries by interviewing 15-year-old students at a school in Doha and posting quotations with their first names on a public blog. The students will be told the interviews are “about school life”. Explain how unethical methods could reduce the value of the findings.
items.answer: Deceived or identifiable participants may not answer honestly, and the report’s credibility would be undermined.
items.markingKey: 1 mark honesty of answers; 1 mark credibility [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that ethical rules make it too difficult for students to research sensitive political issues such as the spread of online disinformation during elections. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: For: Consent and anonymity requirements limit who can be interviewed. Some groups (refugees, officials) may be inaccessible or vulnerable. Against: Secondary sources and anonymised surveys still allow rigorous research. Ethical rules protect participants and make findings more trustworthy. Judgement: Ethics shape the methods rather than preventing research; good design can meet both aims.

items.stem: Priya lives in Santiago and has followed debates about reform of the UN Security Council for two years. A first search finds a report by an intergovernmental organisation such as the UN Development Programme and several news reports, but little local data. Priya wants to research “reform of the UN Security Council” for the research report. (a) Explain why the topic needs to be narrowed. (b) Suggest one way to narrow the topic.
items.answer: (a) “Reform of the UN Security Council” is too broad for 5,000 words; narrowing to a country, group, time period or policy allows depth and a clear debate. (b) Focus on one course of action, e.g. whether the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities, in a specified region.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark too broad; 1 mark how narrowing helps [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: “Feasibility should be the most important factor when choosing a research report topic.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: A topic without accessible evidence cannot be researched properly. Time and word limits are fixed. Against: Without interest, motivation fades over a long project. A topic needs a genuine academic debate and alternative perspectives. Judgement: Feasibility is a necessary condition, but the best topics, e.g. on reform of the UN Security Council, combine interest, debate and access to evidence.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a word in the question, such as “effective” or “responsibility”, whose meaning must be defined and made measurable”?
items.answer: Key term
items.markingKey: Key term: a word in the question, such as “effective” or “responsibility”, whose meaning must be defined and made measurable. [1]

items.stem: A student’s research question is “To what extent is it the responsibility of the riverside governments to address disputes over shared rivers?” Explain why the term “responsibility” must be defined in the report, and suggest how.
items.answer: “Responsibility” can be understood in different ways, so perspectives may talk past each other and the judgement cannot be tested; the student should distinguish legal duty from moral obligation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark ambiguity; 1 mark consequence for judgement; 1 mark sensible definition/criteria [3]

items.stem: A student’s research question is “How effective would it be for the UN member states to add new permanent members such as the G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan) and African states?” Explain why the term “effective” must be defined in the report, and suggest how.
items.answer: “Effective” can be understood in different ways, so perspectives may talk past each other and the judgement cannot be tested; the student should state measurable criteria, e.g. change in turnout or in the number of cases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark ambiguity; 1 mark consequence for judgement; 1 mark sensible definition/criteria [3]

items.stem: Rewrite this research question so that it is focused and permits alternative perspectives: “How can the world solve all political problems?” Explain how your version improves on it.
items.answer: e.g. “Should countries upstream on a shared river need the agreement of downstream countries before building dams?” — the original is far too broad to answer in depth in 5,000 words; the new question is contestable, focused and can be answered using evidence from different perspectives (e.g. the government of Ethiopia and the government of Egypt).
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused question; 1 mark contestable; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: Leila’s proposed research question is: “To what extent is it the responsibility of the richer countries to address migration caused by climate change?” Identify a key term that needs defining and suggest a definition.
items.answer: “responsibility”: distinguish legal duty from moral obligation and say whose responsibility is meant.
items.markingKey: 1 mark term; 1 mark workable definition [2]

items.stem: ““to what extent” questions are always the best form of research question for the research report.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: They invite judgement and the weighing of perspectives. They allow a qualified conclusion. Against: Other forms (“Should…?”, “How far…?”) can be equally contestable. A “to what extent” question can still be vague or too broad. Judgement: The form matters less than focus, contestability and defined terms; e.g. “How effective are anti-corruption agencies at reducing corruption in government contracts?” works without that wording.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that a detailed research proposal is the key to a successful research report on corruption in public procurement? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: It clarifies the question, methods and sources before work begins. A timeline and milestones prevent last-minute work. Against: Research often changes direction as evidence is found, so plans must be flexible. Success depends on the quality of analysis and evaluation, which a plan cannot guarantee. Judgement: A proposal is necessary but not sufficient; it should be revised as the research log records changes.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: What is meant by “aim” in Global Perspectives?
options: A specific, measurable step towards achieving an aim.
The teacher who gives general guidance on the research but does not write or correct the report.
A schedule of research tasks and deadlines.
A broad statement of what the research intends to achieve.
items.answer: A broad statement of what the research intends to achieve.
items.markingKey: Aim: a broad statement of what the research intends to achieve. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a research proposal on the spread of online disinformation during elections should include a section headed “Timeline”.
items.answer: It breaks a long project into deadlines so that research, drafting and editing are all completed on time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark purpose; 1 mark developed/applied [2]

items.stem: Yusuf’s draft research proposal on “How far should governments be able to restrict the media in the name of national security?” contains these sections: Research question, Aims and objectives, Context and rationale, Methods and sources, Timeline. Explain how the supervisor can help without compromising the independence of the research.
items.answer: By giving general feedback on the plan and progress, asking questions and setting deadlines, but not writing, rewriting or correcting the report.
items.markingKey: 1 mark appropriate help; 1 mark limit [2]

items.stem: A student’s report on state use of facial recognition surveillance must be submitted at the end of week 20. Tasks, done in sequence: literature review 4 weeks, primary research 2 weeks, analysis 2 weeks, drafting 5 weeks, editing and referencing 2 weeks. The supervisor advises leaving 2 weeks’ contingency. Calculate the total time needed and the latest week by the end of which the student must start, including the contingency.
items.answer: Total = 15 weeks; with contingency 17 weeks; latest start = end of week 20 − 17 = week 3.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total; 1 mark contingency added; 1 mark latest start [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that a detailed research proposal is the key to a successful research report on the use of economic sanctions.
items.answer: For: It clarifies the question, methods and sources before work begins. A timeline and milestones prevent last-minute work. Against: Research often changes direction as evidence is found, so plans must be flexible. Success depends on the quality of analysis and evaluation, which a plan cannot guarantee. Judgement: A proposal is necessary but not sufficient; it should be revised as the research log records changes.

items.stem: A student plans interviews with people affected by the export of plastic waste to poorer countries. Explain why avoiding deception is important and how the student could ensure it.
items.answer: Avoiding deception means that participants should not be misled about the purpose of the research; this protects participants and the credibility of the research. The student could explain it at the start, record it on a consent form and follow it when storing and reporting data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark why important; 1 mark practical step [3]

items.stem: A student plans interviews with people affected by low voter turnout among young people. Explain why right to withdraw is important and how the student could ensure it.
items.answer: Right to withdraw means that participants can leave the research at any time and have their data removed; this protects participants and the credibility of the research. The student could explain it at the start, record it on a consent form and follow it when storing and reporting data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark why important; 1 mark practical step [3]

items.stem: Amara plans to research the spread of online disinformation during elections by interviewing 15-year-old students at a school in Kathmandu and posting quotations with their first names on a public blog. The students will be told the interviews are “about school life”. Identify two ethical problems with the plan.
items.answer: Deception (true purpose hidden); lack of anonymity (first names published); possible lack of parental consent for under-18s.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2 [2]
